lesson.title: Looping Through Every Character
lesson.summary: Because a string is a sequence, a for loop can walk through it one character at a time, combining String Basics and For Loop into a powerful pattern for character-by-character work.
lesson.body:
A string is a sequence, an ordered collection of characters, and like any sequence in Python it can be looped over directly with a for loop. This chapter connects two ideas you already have: String Basics taught you that a string is built from individual characters accessible by index, and For Loop taught you the general pattern of repeating an action once for each item in a collection. Putting them together, for char in some_string: walks through a string one character at a time, without you needing to manage an index counter yourself.

Trace through this loop with word = "cat":

for char in word:
    print(char)

On the first pass, char is bound to 'c', the character at index 0, and it gets printed. The loop then automatically advances, binding char to 'a', the character at index 1, and printing it. Finally char is bound to 't', the character at index 2, printed, and the loop ends because there are no more characters left. The output is three lines: c, a, t. Notice you never wrote word[0], word[1], word[2] explicitly. The for loop handles the indexing internally, which is both safer, since you cannot accidentally go out of bounds, and more readable.

This pattern becomes genuinely useful when you need to inspect or count something about each character. Consider counting vowels in a word:

word = "banana"
vowel_count = 0
for char in word:
    if char in "aeiou":
        vowel_count += 1
print(vowel_count)  # 3

Tracing this: the loop visits 'b' (not a vowel, skip), 'a' (vowel, count becomes 1), 'n' (skip), 'a' (vowel, count becomes 2), 'n' (skip), 'a' (vowel, count becomes 3). The final count is 3, matching the three letter-a occurrences in "banana". The check char in "aeiou" reuses the in operator against a string, which works because a string is a sequence you can search through, the same underlying idea that makes for char in word possible in the first place.

If you also need the index alongside each character, for instance to report the position where something was found, Python provides enumerate(), which pairs each character with its index: for i, char in enumerate(word): gives you both i (the index, starting at 0) and char (the character) on every pass. This is worth knowing exists, though the plain for char in word form is what you will use most often, since most character-by-character work only cares about the character's value, not its position.

Building a new string out of an old one, one character at a time, is another common pattern, and it connects directly to the Join Method chapter. Suppose you want to remove every space from a sentence:

sentence = "a b c"
letters = []
for char in sentence:
    if char != " ":
        letters.append(char)
result = "".join(letters)
print(result)  # "abc"

Tracing this: the loop visits 'a' (not a space, append it), ' ' (a space, skip it), 'b' (append it), ' ' (skip it), 'c' (append it). After the loop, letters holds ["a", "b", "c"], and "".join(letters) glues them together with an empty separator, producing "abc". This pattern, loop through the characters, decide what to keep, then join the results back into a string, is one of the most common shapes in beginner string-processing code, because strings themselves cannot be built up character by character with append() the way lists can; you must collect the characters in a list first and join them at the end, or build a new string with concatenation at each step.
